extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and authors seeking guidance on character development
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for fiction writers on distinguishing, creating, and placing round (multidimensional) and flat (single-idea) characters in stories, including when to use each and how to craft them effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters are layered / multidimensional
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters have layers. They’re multidimensional. They have depth, and they’re complex figures that the reader can get to know them over the course of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round characters are often the most memorable; examples include Frodo, Mary (The Secret Garden), and Holden Caulfield. This is a core definitional feature used to judge whether a character is round.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters must be built over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters can only be built over time—Forster said they are 'fit to perform tragically for any length of time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character appears only a few pages, you cannot realistically create a round character. Readers need sustained exposure to a character to perceive them as real and layered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters must be capable of surprising convincingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters need to be 'capable of surprising in a convincing way.' Because they are not predictable, the reader feels curious and gets to learn more about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise must be believable in light of the character's layers (example: Superman reversing time is surprising because it reveals an unexpected depth of feeling/power). Flat characters can't surprise because they are perceived as fully known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters need to change (character development visible to reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters need to change in the eyes of the reader—the reader needs to learn something new about the character over the course of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes can be growth, revelation, or moral decline (examples: Dorothy in The Wizard of Oz, Bright Lights, Big City narrator, Fight Club narrator). This change increases intrigue and memorability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters' actions should have explanations (motivations and causality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters’ actions have explanations—actions and traits should be grounded in who they are or events in their past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give plausible causes for behavior (e.g., sulky because of past trauma; exuberant because trying to forget pain; shy because nervous). This connection between motivation and action makes characters believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters need robust backstories
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters need robust backstories—elements like origin, social/economic status, education, family and friends help explain who they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backstory seeps into the story to justify choices and layers (example: Hermione’s Muggle-born status explains her school behavior). Use selective backstory that informs motivation and behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters need internal conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters require internal conflict in addition to external conflict; internal struggle is often the root of complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal conflict makes characters compelling (Macbeth’s ambition vs fear/expectations). Without internal conflict, a character may read flat even if given lots of external action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters should contain contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters have contradictions—'I contain multitudes.' Opposing traits make them feel true to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contradictions (e.g., powerful yet fearful Macbeth) create relatability and depth. Use opposing forces in personality and motivation to create complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters should feel authentic / have 'life within the pages'
rubrics_metrics.description: A round character 'has life within the pages of a book'—they feel like real human beings in their complexity and imperfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity is the culmination of layers, motivations, conflict, change, and contradiction; aim for characters who feel true and human to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters are constructed around a single idea or quality (predictable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are surface-level and one-dimensional; Forster said they ought to be 'constructed round a single idea or quality.' They are predictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters are useful when predictability supports the story. Their predictability distinguishes them from round characters and is a feature, not necessarily a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use flat characters to fill out the world / serve as extras
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters often appear only briefly to fill out the protagonist’s world and add realism without stealing focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rex in Toy Story (adds humor/support), Prim in The Hunger Games (catalyst but predictable), Zazu in The Lion King. These characters expand the world without requiring deep development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters are appropriate for certain genres (fairy tales, parables, Kafka)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some genres call for flat characters—fairy tales, parables, and Kafka-style works often use one-dimensional or archetypal figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In these genres, characters convey ideas or moral lessons rather than psychological realism (examples: Little Red Riding Hood, Kafka’s titled characters, Aesop’s fables). Match character type to genre expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to write flat characters well: communicate trait quickly and clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat means a character is 'action/trait' without much justification—make their defining trait immediately obvious and don’t over-explain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a nosy neighbor shown peeking through curtains with binoculars immediately communicates their type. Flat characters should be easy for audiences to understand at a glance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intentional about a flat character’s function (expand world, advance plot, foil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters should be written consciously with a clear function—expanding the world, advancing the plot, or serving as a foil for main characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If serving as a foil (e.g., Lady Capulet and Lord Montague vs. Romeo and Juliet), keep them consistent with that role and avoid unintended complexity that confuses their purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flat characters 'pretending to be round' (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: The biggest problem is when a character is intended to be round but reads as flat—Forster warned against characters who 'pretend to be round.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fatal error: misplacing an underdeveloped character in a role that requires depth weakens the story. Ensure character development matches their narrative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic vs static: different axis than round vs flat
rubrics_metrics.description: Dynamic/static describe whether a character evolves; they are not synonyms for round/flat. A dynamic character evolves over the story; a static one remains consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dynamic often aligns with round and static with flat, but mixing is possible (e.g., a static character can still be round if richly realized). Use both axes when analyzing or designing characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose round vs flat (role-based guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose round characters for protagonists and leading cast; choose flat characters for background/supporting roles or when writing simple/parable-like stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Round characters engage readers and should occupy central roles; flat characters provide stability, contrast, or genre-appropriate simplicity. Make choices based on character role, story complexity, and genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questionnaire checklist for deciding round vs flat
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of decision questions to determine whether a character should be round or flat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions provided: Does this character appear in a significant portion of the book? How long should it take for the reader to understand this character? Does the character exist simply to fulfill some section of the plot? Does the character need a backstory? How often does this character interact with your protagonist? Do you want this character to be especially memorable? How realistic is this character? Does the character have any internal conflict? Will this character change at all over the course of the story? Will this character surprise the reader?

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance the mix of round and flat characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t attempt to write all round characters; aim for the right mix between round and flat characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making every character round wastes effort and dilutes reader focus. Use different 'shapes' to fit story needs; experimentation helps find the correct balance so readers know which characters to care about.
